story.text: In a speech to his people, the Shang king Pangeng compared good order to a fishing net: when the net is held by its main cord, its strands are in order and do not tangle. That line became the idiom for doing things in an orderly, unhurried way.

use.how: Mostly adverbial before 地 + verb, or as a predicate: 工作进行得有条不紊。 Said of how someone handles tasks, especially under pressure.

near.diff: 井井有条 describes a well-ordered state (a room, accounts); 有条不紊 describes the calm, step-by-step way something is being done.

cue: The fire alarm goes off during an exam; the teacher calmly sends the class out row by row without any panic. How did she handle it?

ctx.s: 她做事一向{有条不紊}，从来不慌。
ctx.en: She always does things calmly and methodically and never panics.

ctx.s: 虽然客人很多，服务员还是{有条不紊}地上菜。
ctx.en: Even with so many guests, the waiters kept serving the dishes in a calm, orderly way.

ctx.s: 停电以后，护士们{有条不紊}地把病人转到了别的楼层。
ctx.en: After the power cut, the nurses moved the patients to other floors calmly and in good order.

ctx.s: 面对记者的提问，新闻发言人{有条不紊}地一一作答。
ctx.en: Faced with the reporters' questions, the spokesperson answered them one by one, calm and methodical.

ctx.s: 婚礼那天乱成一团，多亏你{有条不紊}地安排好了一切。
ctx.en: The wedding day was chaos; thank goodness you calmly arranged everything step by step.

ctx.s: 只剩一个小时了，大家都慌了，只有组长还在{有条不紊}地分配任务。
ctx.en: With only an hour left everyone panicked; only the team leader kept handing out tasks calmly and methodically.

bad.s: 听到坏消息，他{有条不紊}地哭了起来。
bad.en: (meant: he started crying steadily)
bad.why: It describes orderly, methodical handling of tasks, not the manner of an emotional reaction.

bad.s: 我把文件{有条不紊}了。
bad.en: (meant: I put the files in order)
bad.why: It is not a verb that takes an object; to say you sorted the files, use a plain verb meaning tidy up and keep the idiom for the manner.

mean: by the book, following set procedure
lit: to place things by section and put them in their ranks

story.text: The Jin-dynasty writer Lu Ji, describing how a piece of writing is composed, said that the writer chooses ideas and places them in their proper sections, then weighs the words and puts them in their proper ranks. Taken from writing, the phrase came to mean doing anything in its set order, step by step.

use.how: Adverbial (按部就班地做) or predicate. Neutral advice to go step by step, but can criticise rigid routine: 不能再按部就班了。

near.diff: 有条不紊 praises a calm, orderly manner; 按部就班 only says one follows the set steps, and can imply a lack of flexibility.
循序渐进 is gradual progress stage by stage, as in learning; 按部就班 is keeping to an established procedure or routine, sometimes too rigidly.

cue: A new lab assistant wants to skip steps in the standard procedure to save time. You tell him to follow the set procedure exactly, step by step.

ctx.s: 做实验必须{按部就班}，哪一步都不能跳过。
ctx.en: In an experiment you have to follow the procedure in order; you can't skip a single step.

ctx.s: 你先别急，按照说明书{按部就班}地装就行。
ctx.en: Don't rush; just assemble it following the instructions step by step.

ctx.s: 他每天{按部就班}地上班下班，日子过得很平静。
ctx.en: Every day he goes to work and comes home on the same routine, and his life is very quiet.

ctx.s: “这个项目还来得及吗？”“只要{按部就班}地推进，月底前能完成。”
ctx.en: "Can this project still make it?" "As long as we push ahead step by step, it can be done before the end of the month."

ctx.s: 现在情况紧急，不能再{按部就班}了，得想个新办法。
ctx.en: This is an emergency; we can't keep going by the usual procedure, we need a new approach.

ctx.s: 有人批评这家公司过于{按部就班}，缺少创新。
ctx.en: Some people criticise the company for sticking too closely to set routines and lacking innovation.

bad.s: 他突然决定{按部就班}，辞职去旅行了。
bad.en: (meant: he suddenly, on impulse, quit to travel)
bad.why: It means following the set order of steps, the opposite of a sudden impulsive decision.

bad.s: 这个房间收拾得很{按部就班}。
bad.en: (meant: the room is very neatly tidied)
bad.why: It describes going through a process in order, not how tidy a place looks; a neat room calls for a word meaning tidy or well ordered.

lit: because of a disaster, to gain good fortune

story.text: Writing about Guan Zhong, the famous chief minister of the state of Qi, the historian Sima Qian said that in governing he was good at turning disaster into good fortune and turning defeat into success. The idea of drawing good out of a misfortune is the core of this idiom.

use.how: Predicate, often after 真是, 算是 or 反而: 他丢了工作，反而因祸得福。 Said after the good outcome has actually come.

near.diff: 塞翁失马 says a loss may turn out well, often as comfort before the outcome is known; 因祸得福 states that the good has already come from it.

cue: A flood shut her shop, so she moved the business online, and sales went up threefold. How do you sum up what happened to her?

ctx.s: 我被裁员以后自己开了店，没想到{因祸得福}。
ctx.en: After I was laid off I opened my own shop, and it unexpectedly turned out to be a blessing.

ctx.s: 他错过了那班飞机，结果{因祸得福}，躲过了一场事故。
ctx.en: He missed that flight, and the mishap saved him: he escaped an accident.

ctx.s: 腿受伤在家的那几个月，她读完了好多书，也算{因祸得福}吧。
ctx.en: In the months she was home with a hurt leg she read lots of books, so you could say some good came of it.

ctx.s: “听说你搬家是因为房东涨租？”“是啊，不过新家离公司更近，真是{因祸得福}。”
ctx.en: "I heard you moved because the landlord raised the rent?" "Yes, but the new place is closer to work, so it turned out a blessing."

ctx.s: 这次失败让团队发现了产品的大问题，可以说是{因祸得福}。
ctx.en: This failure let the team find a major problem in the product, so it was a blessing in disguise.

ctx.s: 那场大病之后，他戒了烟，开始锻炼，反而{因祸得福}，身体比以前更好了。
ctx.en: After that serious illness he quit smoking and started exercising; it actually did him good, and he is healthier than before.

bad.s: 他中了彩票，真是{因祸得福}。
bad.en: (meant: he won the lottery, what luck)
bad.why: There must first be a misfortune that leads to the good; plain good luck such as a lottery win is just luck.

bad.s: 我丢了钱包，真是{因祸得福}，太倒霉了。
bad.en: (meant: I lost my wallet, what bad luck)
bad.why: It means good came out of the bad, not simply bad luck; to complain about losing a wallet, just say it was unlucky.

mean: to escape from the jaws of death
lit: from inside death, to flee into life

use.how: Predicate or object (经历过死里逃生): 他在车祸中死里逃生。 Said of surviving a real mortal danger such as an accident, disaster or war.

near.diff: 九死一生 stresses how deadly the danger or venture was; 死里逃生 stresses the escape itself.

cue: A climber is buried by an avalanche, digs himself out after hours in the snow, and is found alive. What has he just done?

ctx.s: 那次车祸他{死里逃生}，只受了点轻伤。
ctx.en: He narrowly escaped death in that car crash and was only slightly hurt.

ctx.s: 地震时她被困了三天，最后{死里逃生}。
ctx.en: She was trapped for three days in the earthquake and in the end came out alive.

ctx.s: 船翻了以后，几名渔民抱着木板漂了一夜，终于{死里逃生}。
ctx.en: After the boat capsized, several fishermen clung to planks all night and finally escaped with their lives.

ctx.s: “你还记得那次登山遇到雪崩吗？”“怎么不记得，那可真是{死里逃生}啊。”
ctx.en: "Do you remember the avalanche on that climb?" "How could I forget? We barely got out alive."

ctx.s: 报道说，飞行员在飞机坠毁前跳伞，{死里逃生}。
ctx.en: The report says the pilot parachuted out before the plane crashed and escaped death.

ctx.s: 经历过{死里逃生}的人，往往更懂得珍惜生活。
ctx.en: People who have been through a narrow escape from death often value life more.

bad.s: 爷爷昨天{死里逃生}了，我们明天去参加葬礼。
bad.en: (meant: Grandpa passed away yesterday)
bad.why: It means surviving death, the opposite of dying; using it before mentioning a funeral is a shocking contradiction.

bad.s: 我们{死里逃生}地赶上了最后一班车。
bad.en: (meant: we only just caught the last bus)
bad.why: It is about surviving real mortal danger, not being barely in time for a bus, and it is not used as an adverb with the particle de.

mean: a hopeful new way opening when all seemed lost

story.text: The Song poet Lu You, walking through the countryside, wrote that among the folded hills and winding streams he began to doubt there was any road ahead, when beyond the shady willows and bright flowers another village appeared. The couplet is still quoted for a sudden way out of an impasse.

use.how: Predicate (事情柳暗花明了) or in the full line 柳暗花明又一村. Said of a turn for the better after an apparent dead end.

near.diff: 苦尽甘来 is a long hardship ending and good times arriving; 柳暗花明 is a sudden new way out appearing just when one seemed stuck.

cue: Talks had been stuck for weeks and everyone expected failure; then one new proposal opened everything up again. How did things turn?

ctx.s: 正当我们以为没希望的时候，事情突然{柳暗花明}。
ctx.en: Just when we thought there was no hope, things suddenly opened up.

ctx.s: 找了半年工作都没结果，后来一位老同学推荐了他，总算{柳暗花明}。
ctx.en: Half a year of job hunting got him nowhere; then an old classmate recommended him and at last a way opened.

ctx.s: 谈判陷入僵局，对方第二天却提出了新方案，局面一下子{柳暗花明}。
ctx.en: The talks had reached deadlock, but the next day the other side proposed a new plan and the situation suddenly brightened.

ctx.s: “别灰心，说不定过几天就{柳暗花明}了。”
ctx.en: "Don't lose heart; in a few days a way out may well appear."

ctx.s: 研究卡住了好几个月，一次偶然的实验结果带来了{柳暗花明}的转机。
ctx.en: The research was stuck for months; a chance experimental result brought an unexpected way forward.

ctx.s: 本以为这次肯定失败了，没想到又有了转机，真是山重水复疑无路，{柳暗花明}又一村。
ctx.en: I was sure it had failed, but then things turned around: just when the road seemed to end, a new village came into view.

bad.s: 他一直很顺利，今天又{柳暗花明}了。
bad.en: (meant: things went well for him again today)
bad.why: It needs an apparent dead end first; for progress that has always been smooth, a different idiom about plain sailing fits.

bad.s: 公司倒闭了，大家都感到{柳暗花明}。
bad.en: (meant: everyone felt it was hopeless)
bad.why: It is the turn toward hope, not despair; a company collapsing with no way out is the opposite situation.

mean: at a dead end with nowhere left to turn
lit: walking, with no road left to head for

use.how: Predicate or attributive (走投无路的人); often 被逼得走投无路. Said of a person in desperate straits with no help or way out.

near.diff: 穷途末路 is the end of the road, often for a doomed person or force, and can sound critical; 走投无路 stresses having nowhere to turn for help.

cue: Turned away by every bank and every relative, a man drowning in debt has no one left to ask. Describe his situation.

ctx.s: 他欠了很多钱，已经{走投无路}了。
ctx.en: He owes a lot of money and has nowhere left to turn.

ctx.s: 要不是{走投无路}，谁会去求人呢？
ctx.en: Who would go begging for help unless they had no other way out?

ctx.s: 那年她丢了工作又生了病，几乎{走投无路}。
ctx.en: That year she lost her job and fell ill, and was nearly at the end of her rope.

ctx.s: 被警察包围以后，小偷{走投无路}，只好投降。
ctx.en: Surrounded by the police, the thief had no way out and had to give himself up.

ctx.s: “你为什么来找我？”“我实在是{走投无路}了，只有你能帮我。”
ctx.en: "Why have you come to me?" "I really have nowhere else to turn; only you can help me."

ctx.s: 当年很多{走投无路}的农民只好离开家乡，到城里谋生。
ctx.en: Back then many desperate farmers had no choice but to leave home and seek a living in the cities.

bad.s: 这条小路{走投无路}，我们回去吧。
bad.en: (meant: this lane is a dead end, let's go back)
bad.why: It describes a person's desperate plight, not a road; a lane that leads nowhere is simply a dead end.

bad.s: 生活把他{走投无路}了。
bad.en: (meant: life drove him to despair)
bad.why: It is not a causative verb that takes an object; you must say life forced him (bi de) until he had nowhere to turn.

lit: riding a tiger, it is hard to get off

story.text: When Yang Jian was seizing power at the Northern Zhou court, his wife, later Empress Dugu, sent him word that the great undertaking was already under way: like someone riding a wild beast, he could not get down, so he must press on. He went on to found the Sui dynasty. The image of a rider who cannot dismount became this idiom.

use.how: Predicate, often 弄得骑虎难下 or 我也是骑虎难下. Said of someone who has started something and cannot back out without worse loss or loss of face.

near.diff: 进退两难 is any dilemma where both choices are hard; 骑虎难下 stresses that one has already committed and stopping would be worse.

cue: He boasted he'd start a company; now friends have put money in and pulling out would humiliate him, though he regrets it. His position?

ctx.s: 话已经说出去了，现在他{骑虎难下}。
ctx.en: He has already said it publicly, and now he can't back down.

ctx.s: 投了这么多钱，项目停下来损失更大，公司{骑虎难下}。
ctx.en: So much money has gone in that stopping the project would cost even more; the company is stuck with it.

ctx.s: 他本来只是开玩笑说要跑马拉松，结果大家都当真了，弄得他{骑虎难下}。
ctx.en: He only joked about running a marathon, but everyone took him seriously, and now he can't back out.

ctx.s: “你为什么还在跟他们打官司？”“事情闹到这一步，我也是{骑虎难下}啊。”
ctx.en: "Why are you still suing them?" "It has gone this far; I can't just stop now."

ctx.s: 婚礼请帖都发出去了，她心里后悔，却{骑虎难下}。
ctx.en: The wedding invitations had all gone out; she regretted it inside but felt there was no backing out.

ctx.s: 双方都公开表了态，谁先让步谁就丢面子，现在谁都{骑虎难下}。
ctx.en: Both sides had taken public positions and whoever gave way first would lose face, so neither could back down.

bad.s: 他还没开始做这件事，所以{骑虎难下}。
bad.en: (meant: he hasn't started, so he can't decide)
bad.why: It needs a commitment already made; hesitating before you have even started is simple indecision.

bad.s: 这道题太难了，我{骑虎难下}。
bad.en: (meant: this problem is too hard for me to solve)
bad.why: It is about being unable to back out of something begun, not about a task being too difficult.

mean: easily solved once the key is found
lit: meeting the blade, it splits apart

story.text: During the Jin campaign against the state of Wu, some generals wanted to stop and wait. The commander Du Yu refused: the army's momentum, he said, was like splitting bamboo; once the first few joints are cut, the rest split apart as they meet the blade. He pressed on and Wu fell.

use.how: Predicate with the problem as subject, often after 就 or 都: 问题迎刃而解。 It takes no object.

near.diff: 轻而易举 says a task is easy to do; 迎刃而解 says problems fall away once the key one is dealt with.

cue: Three bugs in an app all came from one wrong setting; once she fixed that setting, all three vanished at once. What happened to the bugs?

ctx.s: 找到原因以后，问题就{迎刃而解}了。
ctx.en: Once we found the cause, the problem solved itself.

ctx.s: 只要把基础打好，后面的难题都会{迎刃而解}。
ctx.en: As long as you build a solid foundation, the harder problems later will all fall into place.

ctx.s: 老师一句提示，我卡了半天的那道题就{迎刃而解}了。
ctx.en: With one hint from the teacher, the problem I'd been stuck on for ages was suddenly easy.

ctx.s: “两个部门一直吵来吵去，怎么办？”“让他们坐下来见一面，很多误会自然{迎刃而解}。”
ctx.en: "The two departments keep arguing; what should we do?" "Get them to sit down together, and many misunderstandings will clear up by themselves."

ctx.s: 资金一到位，招人、租房这些麻烦都{迎刃而解}。
ctx.en: Once the funding came through, hiring, renting space and all those headaches were sorted out at a stroke.

ctx.s: 专家指出，只要解决了人才问题，其他困难都将{迎刃而解}。
ctx.en: The experts point out that once the talent problem is solved, the other difficulties will resolve easily.

bad.s: 我{迎刃而解}了这个问题。
bad.en: (meant: I solved this problem)
bad.why: It takes no object and its subject is the problem itself: the problem resolves, rather than I resolve the problem.

bad.s: 这件事我们费了好几个月的劲，一点一点才{迎刃而解}。
bad.en: (meant: after months of hard work, bit by bit, we finally solved it)
bad.why: It means things resolve easily once the key is found, not after a long, laborious grind of many months.

mean: admirable because it is so hard to do
lit: hard to manage, and so worth prizing

use.how: Predicate (真是难能可贵) or attributive (难能可贵的精神). Praises a person's act or quality that is rare given how hard it is.

near.diff: 来之不易 says a result was hard-won and should be cherished; 难能可贵 praises the act or quality itself as admirably rare.

cue: A single mother working two jobs still studies every night and finishes her degree. How do you praise her for managing something so rare?

ctx.s: 他这么年轻就这么有耐心，真是{难能可贵}。
ctx.en: For someone so young to be so patient is truly admirable.

ctx.s: 在那么困难的条件下坚持读完大学，{难能可贵}。
ctx.en: Sticking with university to the end under such hard conditions is really commendable.

ctx.s: 一个小孩子主动把捡到的钱交给警察，这种做法{难能可贵}。
ctx.en: A small child handing found money to the police on his own is something really to be valued.

ctx.s: “她每个周末都去养老院做志愿者，坚持了五年。”“这可真是{难能可贵}。”
ctx.en: "She has volunteered at the care home every weekend for five years." "That's truly admirable."

ctx.s: 比赛输了，他却第一个去向对手祝贺，这种风度{难能可贵}。
ctx.en: He lost the match but was the first to congratulate his opponent; that kind of sportsmanship is rare and admirable.

ctx.s: 评委认为，这部作品最{难能可贵}的是作者始终保持了真诚。
ctx.en: The judges felt that what is most admirable about this work is that the author stayed sincere throughout.

bad.s: 这件衣服很{难能可贵}，我买不起。
bad.en: (meant: this dress is very expensive, I can't afford it)
bad.why: It praises a person's admirable act or quality, not the price of a thing; for an expensive dress just say it is costly.

bad.s: 他偷懒不做作业，真是{难能可贵}。
bad.en: (meant: it's rare for him to slack off)
bad.why: It is praise for something admirable and hard to do; it cannot describe laziness or anything bad.

mean: after hardship come the sweet times
lit: the bitterness is used up, the sweetness arrives

use.how: Predicate, often with 终于 or 总算; also 苦尽甘来的一天. Said of a person or family whose long hardship has given way to good times.

near.diff: 柳暗花明 is a sudden way out of an impasse; 苦尽甘来 is a long stretch of hardship ending and good times following.

cue: After years of night shifts and debt, a couple finally owns their home and their children are grown and doing well. Sum up their life now.

ctx.s: 熬了这么多年，他们家终于{苦尽甘来}了。
ctx.en: After all these hard years, their family's good times have finally come.

ctx.s: 她年轻时吃了很多苦，现在儿女都很孝顺，总算{苦尽甘来}。
ctx.en: She suffered a lot when she was young; now her children are devoted to her, and the sweet times have come at last.

ctx.s: “再坚持一下，等你毕业了就{苦尽甘来}了。”
ctx.en: "Hang in there a bit longer; once you graduate, the hard part will be over and the good times will come."

ctx.s: 经过多年艰苦创业，这家小工厂终于{苦尽甘来}，订单越来越多。
ctx.en: After years of hard struggle, the little factory has finally come through, with more and more orders.

ctx.s: 爷爷常说，人这一辈子总会有{苦尽甘来}的一天。
ctx.en: Grandpa often says that in every life the day comes when hardship ends and sweetness begins.

ctx.s: 这部电影讲的是一对穷苦夫妻相互扶持、{苦尽甘来}的故事。
ctx.en: The film tells the story of a poor couple who support each other until their hard times give way to happiness.

bad.s: 他从小家里有钱，一直很幸福，真是{苦尽甘来}。
bad.en: (meant: he has always had a happy, comfortable life)
bad.why: It needs a long period of hardship first; a life that was always comfortable has no bitterness to come to an end.

bad.s: 他终于{苦尽甘来}了他的生活。
bad.en: (meant: he finally ended the hardship of his life)
bad.why: It takes no object; the person or their life is the subject, as in: his life has finally come through the hard times.
